section_summary: This section concludes Embassy despatch No. 3634 on Japanese activities in Peru and contains its three enclosures: a list of earlier despatches, a commercial report, and a lengthy confidential consular study. The reports document rapid Japanese gains in Peruvian trade, shipping, immigration, urban commerce, and coastal agriculture, while generally rejecting claims that Chimbote was already becoming a Japanese naval base. They also record arms-for-guano transactions, rumors concerning the Peruvian Steamship Company and Galápagos Islands, anti-Japanese press activity, and proposals for immigration, labor, tariff, and landholding restrictions.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3634 on Japanese activities in Peru—conclusion
subfiles.from: Louis G. Dreyfus, Jr., U.S. Embassy, Lima
subfiles.about: The concluding pages assess guano deliveries to Japan and allegations that Chimbote might become a Japanese naval base.
subfiles.summary: The despatch explains that Peru was expected to deliver more than 50,000 tons of guano in payment for Japanese war matériel purchased during the Leticia dispute, contributing to a domestic shortage. It describes Chimbote as an excellent harbor with a conspicuous Japanese commercial population but notes that reported Japanese control of nearby agriculture was limited. Dreyfus closes by transmitting reports from Commercial Attaché Julian D. Smith and Vice Consul Arthur D. Jukes.

subfiles.title: Partial List of Previous Despatches from Embassy on Japanese Situation in Peru
subfiles.about: The enclosure lists earlier Embassy despatches concerning the Japanese situation in Peru.
subfiles.summary: This single-page enclosure enumerates relevant Embassy despatches from 1926, 1927, 1932, 1933, and 1934. It serves as a chronological cross-reference to the Embassy’s prior reporting on Japanese activities in Peru.

subfiles.title: Japanese Trade Activities in Peru
subfiles.about: The report analyzes the growth, composition, distribution, and effects of Japanese trade with Peru.
subfiles.summary: Smith documents a sharp increase in Japanese imports after 1932, attributing it to low prices, organized trade missions, subsidized shipping, and Japanese-controlled distribution networks. Detailed tables trace competition in cotton textiles, knitwear, hosiery, cement, lamps, pharmaceuticals, toothpaste, and prospective iron and steel sales, while also reviewing growing Peruvian exports of cotton and other commodities to Japan. The report notes Japanese involvement in the Chancay Valley, manufacturing, banking rumors, and retail commerce. It concludes that anti-Japanese sentiment, employment rules, immigration proposals, and demands for tariff protection were intensifying in response to this competition.

subfiles.title: Notes on Japanese Activities in Peru
subfiles.from: Arthur D. Jukes, American Vice Consul
subfiles.about: The confidential report investigates Japanese immigration, shipping, commerce, agricultural penetration, and alleged strategic activity in Peru.
subfiles.summary: Jukes finds allegations that Chimbote was already a Japanese base exaggerated, although he emphasizes the harbor’s exceptional naval qualities and the strength of Japanese petty commerce there. Extensive passenger and cargo tables describe Nippon Yusen Kaisha traffic, wartime cargo allegedly manifested as sanitary equipment, and Japanese negotiations involving the Peruvian Steamship Company; the report also reproduces an N.Y.K. service circular and a Peruvian naval officer’s alarmist continental-defense memorandum. Further sections examine Japanese immigration, Lima businesses, and the growing Japanese control or tenancy of coastal agricultural land, including rumors of consular or cooperative financing. The report records a rising Peruvian press and agrarian campaign for restrictions, reproduces Charles A. Lummis’s article advocating national labor and tenancy quotas, and closes with information on the Japanese-language newspapers Lima Nippo and Pejiho.
